title: Write it again (Jeremiah 36)
hookLine: the king burns the scroll column by column, and Jeremiah dictates it again
carry: there were added besides unto them many like words
last: PLANT THE TREE, SIGN THE LEASE.

lines: THREE OR FOUR COLUMNS AT A TIME.
cards: A penknife. A brazier of coals. A long roll of writing.
It's winter, and King Jehoiakim sits in his winter house with a fire burning on the hearth in front of him.
A man named Jehudi is reading aloud to him from a scroll: every warning Jeremiah has spoken, written down by the scribe Baruch.

Every time Jehudi finishes three or four columns, the king cuts that piece off with the penknife and drops it into the fire. He listens to the whole thing, piece by piece, until the entire scroll is ash.

teach.b: Jeremiah is barred from going to the Temple, so he dictates his words, and Baruch writes them in a roll. Baruch reads it aloud in the Lord's house, on a fast day.

teach.h: SOME BEG THE KING TO STOP.
teach.b: Some officials hear it and are shaken. They tell Baruch: go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and let no one know where you are. Then they tell the king, and he sends for the scroll.

The king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and did not tear their garments. But a few officials, Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah, begged the king not to burn the scroll. He would not listen.
So the fire wins. Or seems to.

Then comes a short instruction, in the King James words: "Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll." Jeremiah dictates, and Baruch writes, all over again.
And the chapter ends with a quiet detail: there were added besides unto them many like words.
The second scroll is longer than the first. That's what this chapter seems to hand down: a king can burn a page, but he can't burn the person who remembers it, or the friend holding the pen.
Jewish custom treats a worn-out Torah scroll with care, burying it rather than throwing it away, and new scrolls are written by hand, letter by letter.
The answer to the knife and the fire is a scribe, a fresh roll, and patience.

how: Jews read Jeremiah 36 among the Latter Prophets, and the scene of Baruch writing at Jeremiah's dictation is often taught alongside the care Jewish tradition gives to handwritten scrolls.

practice: Bring to mind something that slipped away, a recipe from someone who's gone, a story your grandfather told, a plan that burned down, and gather what you can, one piece at a time, the way Jeremiah spoke and Baruch wrote.
Don't worry about getting it exact; if something new arrives that wasn't in the first version, let it in too. If you pray, you can ask for help remembering.
